# Tally × Neatlogs: audit and implementation plan

**Audited:** 11 October 2026  
**Repository:** `Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack`, branch `codex/first-user-integrations`  
**Scope:** Read-only source audit, current Neatlogs documentation/API contract, and the neatHack requirements. No source changes, test runs, issue creation, PRs, or remote writes were made.

## Executive assessment

There is real Neatlogs integration code in Tally, but it is not yet a working, end-to-end observability loop on this machine. The code has two distinct ideas:

1. Tally emits its own traces for sizing/routing/escalation decisions and attempt history.
2. Neatlogs’ Codex hooks are intended to capture the actual coding-agent turn: model phases, tool calls, failures, and subagent work.

The second is the evidence judges and Tally users need most. On the audited host, the project’s local SDK packages exist, but no Neatlogs credentials/configuration or Codex hooks are installed. So a live Tally run here is not currently set up to send Tally traces or capture the AO-launched Codex worker.

Even when configured, the application-side traces are shallow: several separate decision traces, a separate nearly empty history trace per attempt, and one trace per five-second ceiling poll. They do not yet form a coherent task/run trace that shows the whole path from issue intake through model/tool work, verification, escalation, and PR. The dashboard stores and displays trace IDs but the run code leaves their URL fields null. The only intended decision feedback from remote Neatlogs data is aggregate pass-rate/cost history; that read path currently requests 100 traces even though the current API caps trace pages at 50, then silently falls back to local history.

The blunt assessment: **Tally has built a Neatlogs transport and some trace hooks, but has not yet turned Neatlogs into a product capability.** The next work should first unblock the first-user setup, then capture one complete, correlated task attempt, then use the trace to explain and measure a before/after improvement.

## What is the source of truth today?

| Data | Current authority | Neatlogs’ role |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub backlog and published PR | GitHub | Not authoritative |
| Run/task status, verification result, attempt ledger, recorded per-attempt spend estimate | Tally’s local `.tally/runs/<run-id>/run.json` and `ledger.json` | Evidence/correlation only |
| Live budget/spend when cfo.ai is enabled | cfo.ai, with Tally’s local integer-nanos ledger and fallback CSV | Not authoritative |
| Local routing history | `.tally/history.json` beside the Tally config | Persistent local fallback and writer |
| Shared routing history, when a read token and project ID are configured | A remote aggregate of recent Neatlogs trace records, preferred over local history when it returns observations | Can affect which tier Tally selects; currently brittle and likely falling back due to an API page-size mismatch |
| Worker prompts, tool calls, model phases, and subagent work | Codex hook events, if the Neatlogs Codex hook is installed in the environment that runs AO workers | Neatlogs stores and presents the actual worker trace |
| Entire checkpoints and handoff context | Entire IDs/metadata plus local ledger | Separate evidence; not a Neatlogs source of truth |

The repo README describes the local ledger and verification as persisted run evidence, and says cfo.ai is the live accounting authority when enabled. `engine/real.ts` writes the run and ledger files; `engine/output.ts` mirrors the latest run. `adapters/history-file.ts` persists the local pass-rate/cost cells.

Neatlogs has two credentials with different jobs. `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` is used to send traces. `NEATLOGS_TOKEN` plus `NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID` is optional read access for the Public API and remote history/readback. Current Neatlogs docs explicitly say SDK ingest credentials do not grant Public API reads; the API uses project-bound service-account/OAuth credentials and scoped access ([authentication and scopes](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/authentication)).

## What code uses Neatlogs now?

### 1. Tally’s own SDK traces

`adapters/neatlogs.ts` lazily imports the `neatlogs` TypeScript SDK and initializes it as workflow `tally-cfo-agent`, tagged `tally` and `cfo-agent`. Its generic `TracePort.span()` always opens a `CHAIN` trace, passes the same small attribute map as both input and attributes, runs a callback, and tries to extract the trace ID from the active W3C carrier. Export failures are intended not to execute application work twice or fail the run.

The `TracePort` is passed through `agent/trace.ts` into:

- `agent/sizer.ts`: `tally.size`
- `agent/router.ts`: `tally.route`
- `agent/baseline.ts`: `tally.baseline.route`
- `agent/escalation.ts`: `tally.escalate`
- `agent/watcher.ts`: `tally.ceiling.poll`

Those are useful starting points. Neatlogs’ TypeScript SDK supports nested spans, explicit trace roots, custom attributes, sessions, and flush/shutdown; a trace is most useful when the actual workflow tree is represented, not merely when an SDK call succeeds ([TypeScript SDK](https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/typescript), [trace concepts](https://docs.neatlogs.com/docs/features/traces)).

### 2. Attempt-history traces and routing feedback

After an attempt finishes, `engine/real.ts:recordHistory()` first writes the outcome to the configured history writer. For a real run with Neatlogs enabled, it then emits an empty callback named like `tally.history.record size=... tier=... result=... cost_nanos=...` with attempt attributes. The trace name itself encodes the outcome. Dry runs do not emit this trace.

When optional read access is present, `NeatlogsPriceHistory.lookup()` lists traces for `tally-cfo-agent`, parses observations from the trace name (and sometimes spans), averages pass rate/cost by task size and tier, and uses that remote aggregate if any matching observations exist. Otherwise it falls back to `.tally/history.json`. `record()` still writes to the local fallback; the SDK trace is the path that places the remote observation in Neatlogs.

There is a high-confidence contract mismatch here: `NeatlogsPriceHistory` defaults to `limit=100`, but the current Public API contract sets `GET /api/v1/public/traces` to a maximum page size of 50. The code catches a failed request and silently returns local history, so a user can believe shared Neatlogs history is influencing routing when it is not. The current API also uses cursor pagination; Tally does not follow cursors in this adapter. This is verifiable from the live contract ([List traces](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/endpoints/traces/get_api_v1_public_traces), [pagination](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/pagination)).

The other weakness is data quality: remote history is grouped only by `(size, tier name)`. It does not distinguish model/version, harness, route-policy version, repository/task family, or price-schedule version. Old outcomes can therefore influence a new model or configuration. It has no freshness or minimum-sample provenance surfaced to the planner.

### 3. Actual Codex worker traces

The repo depends on `@neatlogs/codex` and has `NeatlogsWorkerSpoolAdapter` and `NeatlogsWorkerTraceReader`:

- The Codex hook writes OTLP spans to a local spool.
- After an AO worker finishes, Tally drains selected batches outside the worker sandbox.
- Tally then optionally queries the Public API to verify a readable worker trace and saves its ID in the ledger.
- `engine/trace-recovery.ts` can retry a failed worker-trace drain/readback for a finished run.

This is the strongest sponsor-product fit. The current Codex integration documents one trace per main-thread user prompt, including model phases, tool calls, and subagent work, and documents a local/project setup alternative to global setup ([Codex Hooks](https://docs.neatlogs.com/integrations/codex)).

However, the hook has to be installed where the AO-launched Codex process actually runs. On the audited host, the workspace has `neatlogs@1.1.28` and `@neatlogs/codex@0.1.1` (both the current registry versions observed on 11 October), but the hook status reported `hooksFileExists: false` and `apiKeyConfigured: false`; `~/.codex/hooks.json`, `~/.config/neatlogs/config.json`, and `~/.tally/.env` were absent. The Codex hook is therefore **not configured here**, despite the dependency being installed in the project. If AO runs Codex in another environment, inspect/configure that worker host instead.

The current worker readback also relies on string matching: `NeatlogsWorkerTraceReader` requires the trace’s session ID to equal the Entire native session ID and looks for `Tally run ..., task ..., attempt ...` inside `workflowName`/`traceName`. The Codex hook currently derives workflow name from the prompt and truncates it to 80 characters. Tally puts a correlation sentence in the prompt, but a durable explicit attribute would be safer than relying on a display-name convention. The current code/tests assume this mapping; a real worker trace from this host has not been available to verify it.

### 4. Status and dashboard

The project has a known first-user-flow bug in open issue [#89: Skip disabled neatlogs in tally doctor](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/issues/89), found while working toward [#88: Validate the first-user Tally flow](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/issues/88). `engine/doctor.ts` reports the Neatlogs key as missing even when Neatlogs is disabled; the CLI treats a missing line as failure. That makes an optional sponsor integration block unrelated first-time setup.

Trace IDs are represented separately in the ledger as a decision trace ID and a worker trace ID, which is good. But the code sets `traceUrl` and `workerTraceUrl` to `null`, and `dashboard/app.js` falls back to copyable IDs instead of opening the corresponding Neatlogs trace. The integration status is also too coarse to tell these states apart: SDK initialized, Tally trace exported, worker hook captured, worker batch drained, and worker trace read back.

## How badly are we using Neatlogs?

1. **The live integration is not configured on this host.** There is no key/config or hook file, so there is no evidence of current application or worker traces reaching Neatlogs from here.
2. **The Tally SDK traces are fragments, not an end-to-end run.** Each generic `span()` creates a top-level `CHAIN` trace when there is no common parent. A run’s sizing/routing/escalation/verification/PR work cannot be followed as one coherent tree.
3. **The worker trace—the most valuable data—is optional and not yet demonstrated.** The spool and readback path exist, but the hooks are not installed here and correlation depends on session/name assumptions.
4. **The watcher is over-instrumented.** `CeilingWatcher.poll()` is traced each time it runs (every five seconds during a live attempt). This can create a stream of low-value one-operation traces while still omitting a clean attempt summary. Record the final usage and the ceiling-crossing event on the attempt trace instead.
5. **The history trace is acting like a database row encoded in a trace name.** It has no children and no agent/model/tool activity. It is a workaround, not meaningful observability.
6. **Remote history may never be read.** `limit=100` violates the current endpoint’s maximum of 50; the catch-all fallback hides the failure. Even corrected, missing cursors, repeated uncached API calls, and thin metadata make the result fragile.
7. **The remote feedback is too broad to safely route on.** `(size, tier name)` is insufficient when model/harness/pricing/policy changes; no age/minimum-sample guard or source is shown to users.
8. **No trace-to-product loop exists yet.** Worker trace IDs are not used by sizing, escalation, verification, dashboard links, detection rules, or evaluations. The only remote feedback loop is the limited price-history aggregate.
9. **The UI makes the evidence hard to inspect.** IDs can be copied, but the run dashboard does not provide direct links to the decision and worker traces.
10. **The setup blast radius is unnecessarily broad by default.** Tally asks whether to install global Claude Code and Codex hooks, which traces every session on the machine. Neatlogs supports project-scoped Codex setup; prefer that when it works with AO worktrees, and make global setup an explicit opt-in with an explanation. Since hooks can capture prompts and tool inputs/outputs, keep data scope and local masking visible in the choice. Neatlogs distinguishes local SDK masking from server-side redaction; server settings alone do not protect data before it leaves the process ([PII Redaction](https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/pii-redaction)).

## Target integration design

Keep Tally’s local run state/ledger authoritative for task outcome and spend accounting. Use Neatlogs as the inspectable trace/evaluation layer around an attempt, and use remote history only as a bounded, versioned planning signal.

### Trace shape

For the first useful version, make one Tally-owned root trace per task, with `sessionId = runId` so tasks from one multi-task run group together. Use a `WORKFLOW` root and nest spans underneath it:

```text
tally.task (WORKFLOW; sessionId=runId)
├── intake / impact (TOOL or RETRIEVER)
├── size and route (CHAIN)
├── attempt 1 (TOOL: ao worker lifecycle)
│   ├── Codex worker trace (linked by stable run/task/attempt IDs)
│   ├── budget checks (GUARDRAIL; summarize, do not emit every poll)
│   ├── checkpoint / handoff (TOOL)
│   └── verify (GUARDRAIL)
├── escalation decision (CHAIN)
├── attempt 2 (if present)
└── publish PR and reconcile spend (TOOL)
```

The actual Codex trace should retain the rich model/tool/subagent spans supplied by the official hook package. Link it to the Tally-owned task trace with stable `tally.run_id`, `tally.task_id`, and `tally.attempt` attributes, plus the saved worker trace ID. Do not make a prompt prefix or trace display name the permanent join key. True parent-child continuity across the AO process boundary can be a later spike using Neatlogs’ W3C `injectTraceContext`/`extractTraceContext`, but only if AO can pass that context safely and the hook can consume it; linked traces are a valid first milestone.

### Recommended attributes

Keep attributes small, typed, and useful for filtering. Do not attach the whole GitHub issue, repository files, patch, or command output to the Tally-owned spans by default.

- Run: `tally.run_id`, `tally.mode`, `tally.backlog_source`, `tally.budget_source`, `tally.policy_version`.
- Task: `tally.task_id`, `tally.task_size`, `tally.size_source`, `tally.impact_files_count`, `tally.impact_dependents`, `tally.tests_present`.
- Route: chosen tier/model/harness, estimated pass rate, observed sample count, expected cost, ceiling, and whether the source was local history, remote history, or prior.
- Attempt: attempt number, model/tier, AO status, result category, tokens, estimated cost, cost source, duration, escalation outcome, verifier pass/fail, changed-file count, PR-created boolean.
- Worker link: native session ID and verified worker trace ID; avoid logging credentials or raw session transcripts in Tally metadata.

The coding-agent hook intentionally captures richer prompt/tool evidence; make that consent explicit and verify its actual host. Neatlogs documents that the hook emits model/tool/session context and redacts common secret-bearing fields, but its presence is not a reason to send private repository content indiscriminately ([Codex Hooks](https://docs.neatlogs.com/integrations/codex), [PII Redaction](https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/pii-redaction)).

## Action plan, in order

### P0 — Make first-user setup honest and unblocked

1. Address existing issue #89: when `integrations.neatlogs` is false, `tally doctor` should report `off` (or omit the check) and not fail. Require a Neatlogs key only when the user enabled Neatlogs.
2. Split Neatlogs status into distinct checks: write key present/probe passed; SDK available; Codex hook installed on the AO worker host; worker spool drained; Public API readback verified. Do not report “connected” as proof that the application emitted a trace.
3. Keep the ingest key and service-account read token separate in prompts and status. Public API read access is optional; lack of it must not block trace ingestion.
4. Prefer project-scoped Codex hooks where AO’s worker worktrees load them. If they do not, explain that global installation covers every local session and ask for that choice explicitly.
5. Verify the installed SDK’s local Doctor and a synthetic authenticated probe according to the current Doctor docs. Label this as pipeline/credential verification only: Neatlogs states that a synthetic probe does not prove the user’s application ran or produced a trace ([SDK Doctor](https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/doctor)).

**P0 acceptance:** With Neatlogs off and no Neatlogs secrets, `tally doctor` and the guided first-user flow succeed. With Neatlogs on, the UI identifies separately whether Tally telemetry and worker tracing are configured, without printing secrets or claiming a real trace before one is read back.

### P1 — Capture one useful task trace

1. Refactor the generic trace port so a task-level `WORKFLOW` root can stay active while sizer/router/escalation/verifier spans run beneath it. Use SDK-documented span kinds rather than forcing every operation through the same `CHAIN` wrapper.
2. Wrap the worker lifecycle and verifier/publisher calls with Tally-owned spans. Record start/wait/final usage/stop/failure/verification outcomes and a concise error category. Preserve the current rule that telemetry failure never reruns work or converts a successful task into failure.
3. Remove per-poll trace creation. Keep the ceiling watcher’s safety behavior, but emit a single attempt summary plus a budget-stop event/attributes.
4. Give worker traces explicit correlation attributes or a supported metadata bridge. Verify the relationship among AO session ID, Codex `session_id`, and Entire `entireSessionId`; do not equate them without observing a real trace.
5. Populate trace URLs after successful readback and make both decision/worker evidence clickable from the run dashboard. Keep the ID available as fallback.

**P1 acceptance:** One real, harmless test task produces a Tally task trace with route, attempt, verification, and result spans; a separately captured Codex trace contains its LLM/tool work and matches the same run/task/attempt; the local ledger outcome agrees with both; the dashboard opens both traces. Export failure leaves the local ledger correct and visible.

### P2 — Make remote history correct before it can influence routing

1. Change the list request to a legal page size (at most 50) and implement bounded cursor pagination using the opaque `data.page.nextCursor` exactly as returned. Set a hard page/trace ceiling.
2. Cache one remote history snapshot for the duration of a run instead of re-fetching the same trace list for every size/tier lookup. Batch or bound per-trace span reads and handle 401/403/429/5xx distinctly.
3. Store outcome fields as structured attributes rather than encoding the main record in `traceName`. Version the record schema and include model, harness, pricing/policy version, task size, result, cost, and timestamp.
4. Do not let remote history override local observations unless it is fresh, has a minimum sample count, and matches the current model/harness/policy identity. Show the source, age, and observation count in `tally run --plan` and the decision trace. Keep local `.tally/history.json` as the offline fallback and the local audit record.
5. If reliable shared history is not achievable within the hackathon, keep it out of routing and use Neatlogs for trace inspection and before/after evaluation instead. A narrower truthful integration is better than silently calling stale/incompatible history “connected.”

**P2 acceptance:** Contract-shaped fixtures prove the API request never exceeds 50, cursor pages are read up to a configured ceiling, remote failures are observable and fall back safely, and a plan clearly reports which history source actually informed a route.

### P3 — Use Neatlogs to improve the agent, not just retain telemetry

1. In the Neatlogs project, create a saved view/filter for Tally task traces and detections for useful anomalies: budget ceiling crossed, failed verification, repeated tool failure, unusually high cost/latency, and worker trace missing. Current detections support rules on span content and numeric/boolean attributes ([Detections](https://docs.neatlogs.com/docs/features/detections)).
2. Review one failed or escalated worker trace in Investigate: ask which step failed, what the agent saw, what tool response caused the failure, and whether the retry used the prior work. Keep the conclusions tied to linked evidence ([Investigate](https://docs.neatlogs.com/docs/features/ai-search)).
3. Add a small human/AI evaluation rubric for coding tasks: requirement coverage, test result, scope discipline, correct recovery/escalation, and cost. Score actual task traces rather than synthetic probe traces. Neatlogs’ evaluation workflow can collect structured judgments and aggregate them ([Evals](https://docs.neatlogs.com/docs/features/evals/human-evaluators)).
4. Use trace findings to make one concrete agent improvement—such as a better route threshold, handoff instruction, or verification recovery—and compare the matched before/after run evidence.

## How to measure “how much better”

No honest percentage can be promised before a matched benchmark. Instrumentation itself improves debuggability and judge-verifiable evidence; it does not automatically make the coding agent more accurate or cheaper. Measure the product change with the same issue set, base commit, model choices, verifier, and budget conditions:

- task pass rate;
- cost per passed task and total cost;
- median time to verified completion;
- first-attempt pass rate;
- escalation rate and recovery rate after first-attempt failure;
- percentage of real attempts with both a Tally trace and a worker trace;
- percentage of attempts whose trace result agrees with the local ledger.

Use `tally run --baseline --only <task>` and `tally run --only <task>` on the same isolated target/commit, recording each result. The existing `tally experiment` supports simulated comparisons, but the README says real experiment execution is currently gated; dry-run telemetry is also intentionally not exported. Do not present simulation as proof of live Neatlogs or agent improvement.

For a tiny hackathon benchmark, one matched issue before/after is acceptable as a concrete demo, but describe it as one example. If time permits, repeat several representative tasks and show a table with the numerator/denominator and exact spend. Neatlogs traces should let a judge inspect *why* the outcome changed, not just see a claimed percentage.

## neatHack fit and evidence checklist

The official neatHack page currently says all projects must use neatlogs, Entire, and cfo.ai with clear roles; it asks teams to trace runs and compare before/after; its evidence examples include trace links/screenshots, Entire checkpoints/graph, a cfo.ai business plan, and a failure-recovery run. Published weights are agent 30%, sponsor-tool use 25%, demo video 20%, building in public 15%, and usefulness/originality 10%. The page calls for a public code repository and a demo of three minutes or less, with all three products explicitly covered ([official neatHack requirements and judging](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon)).

For Tally, present the sponsor roles as:

- **Neatlogs:** the evidence layer for a coding-agent task—what the worker was asked, model/tool steps, where it failed, cost/latency, what changed on retry, and how verification ended.
- **Entire:** code graph/checkpoint context used to size work and continue a failed attempt.
- **cfo.ai:** the business plan/unit economics and, where configured, the budget/spend authority.

Before recording the demo, collect:

- one working worker trace and one Tally task trace, both linked from the run;
- one matched before/after task with exact cost/result/latency numbers;
- one real recovery/escalation trace showing the next action after a failure;
- an Entire graph/checkpoint artifact and cfo.ai pricing/cost/revenue/runway plan;
- public commits made during the hackathon and a short `#neatHack` progress post;
- a three-minute walkthrough that shows the agent completing the task, then uses Neatlogs to explain one failure or improvement.

The page currently lists submissions opening 12 October at 7:00 PM IST and a planned close at 11:55 PM IST, with the final cutoff announced on Discord. It also says planning can happen ahead of time but code must be written during the event. Confirm the final cutoff and eligibility against the live event page/Discord before submission; this audit does not certify that the repository history meets that rule.

## Implementation verification checklist

When implementation is authorized, add focused tests and then verify a real application trace (the audit itself did not run tests):

- Doctor: disabled integration is `off`; enabled-but-missing key is actionable; enabled key is not called connected until the agreed probe succeeds.
- SDK adapter: one task root, nested spans, meaningful final attributes, stable error behavior, and no duplicate worker execution on exporter failure.
- Watcher: polling does not emit one trace per tick; ceiling crossing is visible once with final usage/cost.
- Worker hook: explicit consent/setup, correct AO execution host, hook trusted, spool drained, and readback matched by stable run/task/attempt metadata.
- Public API: valid `limit <= 50`, cursor pagination, project-scoped read token, bounded work, retries/rate limits, and visible remote/local history provenance.
- Dashboard: direct links open the correct Tally and worker traces; IDs remain available when links cannot be formed.
- End-to-end: actual run trace agrees with `run.json`/`ledger.json`; synthetic Doctor probe is reported separately from application-trace verification.
- Evidence: save a before/after pair and the measurements used in the demo.

## Source-code map

- `adapters/neatlogs.ts` — SDK init, trace wrapper, export status, flush.
- `agent/trace.ts`; `agent/sizer.ts`; `agent/router.ts`; `agent/escalation.ts`; `agent/watcher.ts` — current Tally decision spans.
- `engine/real.ts` — adapter wiring, history recording, AO worker lifecycle, worker trace drain/readback, ledger fields.
- `adapters/neatlogs-worker-spool.ts` and `adapters/neatlogs-worker-traces.ts` — local hook spool and Public API verification.
- `adapters/neatlogs-history.ts` and `adapters/history-file.ts` — remote aggregate and local history fallback.
- `onboarding/neatlogs.ts`; `engine/doctor.ts`; `engine/env.ts` — keys, onboarding, setup status, secret path.
- `engine/output.ts`; `schema/types.ts`; `dashboard/app.js` — persisted evidence and trace link presentation.
- `engine/trace-recovery.ts` — retrying worker trace drain/readback after a finished run.
- `README.md` — intended integration contract and first-live-run sequence.

## Audit notes

The repository already had a modified `package-lock.json` when this read-only audit began; it was not changed. No real Neatlogs project credential was available, so this report does not claim that any live trace, API read, or remote project setting was verified. Current SDK/package versions and the Neatlogs docs/API contract were checked on 11 October 2026.

# Tally × neatHack: built-in-public strategy and message kit

**Prepared:** 11 October 2026, 4:42 PM IST  
**Project:** Tally — a budget and verification layer for coding-agent work  
**Purpose:** A practical public-engagement plan, ready-to-edit message drafts, and a short user-problem questionnaire for the neatHack build window.  
**Handling:** This file is in `/home/adot/Downloads`, outside the project repository. It is a draft only: no Discord, X, mentor, or sponsor messages have been sent, and no repository files were changed.

## 1. The campaign in one page

### The audience problem

Coding agents can take on repository work, but delegating a backlog creates operational questions: Which issue is safe to hand off? How much might it cost? Did the change pass the repository’s own check? What happens after a failed attempt? Can a maintainer review the work and its cost afterward?

### Tally’s current product story

Tally is an early-build “CFO for a fleet of coding agents.” It is designed to take labeled GitHub issues, estimate task difficulty, route each task to a suitable model tier, enforce per-task spend ceilings, escalate failed work, verify results with the repository’s test command, and keep an attempt-and-cost ledger. Real workers currently run through Agent Orchestrator (AO). Tally’s seven-task quick demo uses simulated workers; it demonstrates the workflow but does not prove live worker quality or economics. The README says the npm package is not released yet. Keep those distinctions visible in every public claim. [Project README](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/blob/main/README.md)

### The public narrative

> **We’re testing whether a maintainer can delegate a small GitHub backlog to coding agents while keeping task selection, spend limits, verification, and recovery visible.**

Use a repeatable update pattern:

1. **Problem:** Name a real coordination or trust failure in agent-driven repository work.
2. **Build:** Show one specific thing Tally now does, or one thing that broke.
3. **Evidence:** Show a run, trace, check result, ledger row, issue, or short screen recording. Label simulated evidence as simulated.
4. **Question:** Ask one focused question that helps the product or its implementation.
5. **Follow-up:** Reply with what changed because of the feedback.

The goal is useful public learning and genuine discussion. Don’t optimize for raw post count, likes, or sponsor tags.

## 2. What the hackathon rewards and what that means for this plan

The current [official neatHack page](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon) lists judging weights of 30% agent performance, 25% use of neatlogs/Entire/cfo.ai, 20% demo video, 15% building in public, and 10% usefulness/originality. For the public-building category, it asks for links to project updates tagged `#neatHack`. The separate community award looks at content quality, shares and discussion, genuine engagement, and whether people want to try or talk about the project; audience size does not decide it. The page says bought likes or bot activity can disqualify a team and that spam in Discord is prohibited.

The page currently lists the submission window as **Monday, 12 October, 7:00–11:55 PM IST**, with the final cutoff to be announced on Discord. Submission is a public quote of the official neatlogs post on X, with team, project, public repository, and demo link. The demo must be three minutes or less and explicitly explain neatlogs, Entire, and cfo.ai. Confirm the cutoff and the official submission post in Discord on the day; the planned close is not the final authority. The page also says neatlogs and cfo.ai will engage with the first 50 quote tweets, so have the final materials ready before the window opens.

**Practical implication:** build a small trail of specific, helpful updates over the remaining build window, then make one clean official submission quote post. Don’t flood the server or X with nearly identical “please support us” posts.

## 3. Positioning and claim discipline

### One-line description

**Tally helps maintainers delegate GitHub issues to coding agents with per-task budgets, verification, escalation, and a spend ledger.**

### Short description

**Tally is an early-build coordinator for coding-agent work. It reads a labeled backlog, estimates and routes tasks, applies spend ceilings, escalates failures, runs the repository’s configured check, and records task outcomes and spend.**

### Use these distinctions in public

| Safe to say from the current README | Only say after you have captured the evidence |
|---|---|
| The quick demo uses simulated workers. | “Tally completed a real repository issue end to end.” |
| Real workers use AO and require a configured coding agent, GitHub CLI access, and a repository test command. | “Tally reduced cost / improved success rate / saved time.” Include the baseline, after run, exact task/config, and measurements. |
| Tally records attempt and verification evidence; optional sponsor integrations have setup requirements. | “Every worker action is visible in Neatlogs.” Link a real, readable trace from the actual worker run. |
| The first-user integration flow is an active validation milestone in [issue #88](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/issues/88). | “Tally is production-ready,” “works with any agent,” or “zero overruns.” These are not supported by the README. |
| The package is not released to npm. GitHub install instructions are in the README. | “Install with npm” unless and until the package is published. |

Before every post, confirm the current branch, running build, trace access, integration configuration, and whether a real run has happened. A local screenshot is not proof of a remote trace; a simulated run is not proof of real model cost or coding quality.

## 4. Channel strategy

| Channel | Audience | Best use | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| neatHack Discord community/project channel | Other builders and potential users | Validate the pain, share a concise progress log, ask for a few targeted testers or reviewers | One initial post, then one meaningful update when there is new evidence; follow channel rules |
| Sponsor-specific Discord channels | Neatlogs, Entire, cfo.ai, and AO practitioners | Ask one concrete technical/product question tied to actual use of that sponsor’s product | Post only where relevant; no copy-paste campaign across channels |
| Assigned mentor | Experienced reviewer with limited time | Ask for a decision on target user, demo focus, or missing proof | One short context-rich message; one follow-up with the result |
| X | Developers, maintainers, agent builders, hackathon audience | Share concise build notes, useful findings, and the final demo; tag `#neatHack` | Two or three distinct posts over the build window, plus the required final quote post |
| Existing personal/team network | People who have actually delegated coding work | Obtain real anecdotes and ask for questionnaire responses or a short conversation | Personal, contextual asks; no mass unsolicited DMs |

### Before posting the next update

The exact earlier post links were not supplied in this request and are not recorded in the repository. Spend ten minutes collecting the links to what the team has already posted on X/Discord. Record date, channel, question asked, and response. Make the next post a follow-up with a new fact or decision, and link the earlier post where it helps continuity. Don’t repeat the same launch announcement.

### What to capture with each update

Prefer one legible artifact: a short GIF/video of a run, a sanitized trace screenshot, a ledger row, a test result, a GitHub issue/PR, or a small architecture sketch. Say what it shows in plain language. Crop or redact repository secrets, access tokens, personal data, private issue titles, and any prompt or output the team is not authorized to publish.

## 5. Short time plan (IST)

The timing below is based on the current event page and the clock at preparation time. Re-check Discord for event announcements and the final deadline.

### Sunday, 11 October — establish the problem and invite feedback

**Now:** Review prior posts; select one current demo clip or screenshot; create the short form in section 6. Post one problem-validation question in the appropriate Discord channel and one distinct X update. Do not wait for a polished launch asset.

**Later today:** Send the mentor note in section 7. If useful, ask one sponsor-specific technical question in the relevant channel. Update the running notes with answers and any implementation decision they caused.

**By end of day:** Report the product’s real status plainly: simulated demo versus real AO validation, what works, what is still under test, and the next milestone. If no real run or Neatlogs trace is available yet, say that directly and use the next block to produce or troubleshoot evidence rather than imply it exists.

### Monday, 12 October — publish evidence and submit

**Morning / early afternoon:** Run the narrowest useful real validation the team can safely complete. Capture the exact task, configuration, test outcome, attempt count, and spend source. If real validation is blocked, capture the blocker and show the simulated demo with a clear label. Publish a progress update only after verifying what it says.

**Before 7:00 PM:** Freeze the short demo, public repository URL, team/project names, and evidence links. Verify each URL in a signed-out/private browser where practical. Keep the demo at three minutes or less and explicitly show the role and result for neatlogs, Entire, and cfo.ai. Do not wait for the last few minutes to render or upload the video.

**At/after submissions open:** Find the official neatlogs submission post, use the official quote-post flow, include team/project/repo/demo, and publish before the cutoff announced on Discord. Save the public URL. The separate draft window is not a submission. Avoid posting a second competing submission.

**After the quote post:** Share it once in the allowed project/community channel with a short explanation and a real request for people to try or critique the demo. Reply to comments with useful answers; don’t ask people to like/repost in exchange for anything.

### After the event

Within a day or two, publish a concise retrospective: what users said, what the team learned, what worked, what failed, and what will be built next. Keep this distinct from the submission and don’t claim outcomes the evidence doesn’t show.

## 6. User-problem questionnaire

### Form title

**How do you manage coding-agent work on a repository?**

### Intro text

> We’re researching how developers delegate repository tasks to coding agents and how they keep spend and results under control. This short form should take about 2–3 minutes. We’re building Tally, an early tool for routing GitHub issues to coding agents with budgets, verification, escalation, and an attempt ledger. We want to learn about your actual workflow, including cases where agents are not useful. Please don’t include private repository URLs, source code, credentials, or personal data. Responses will be summarized for product research; sharing a contact address for follow-up is optional.

### Questions and suggested response types

1. **Which best describes your work?** *(Choose one)*  
   Software developer/maintainer; engineering lead/manager; founder/indie builder; AI-agent/tool builder; student/learner; other; prefer not to say.

2. **How often have you used a coding agent on a real repository task in the last 3 months?** *(Choose one; skip the remaining workflow questions if “never”)*  
   Never; once; less than monthly; monthly; weekly; several times a week or daily.

3. **Think of the most recent repository task you gave an agent. What was the task, and what happened?** *(Short paragraph; ask for a sanitized description, not a repo link.)*

4. **What did you personally have to do before, during, or after the agent worked?** *(Select all that apply)*  
   Choose/split the task; inspect code/context; choose the model/tool; set or estimate a budget; watch the run; handle a failed attempt; review the diff; run tests; redo/revert work; calculate or explain cost; nothing beyond the initial request; other.

5. **How do you currently decide that agent work is safe to accept?** *(Select all that apply)*  
   Automated tests/type checks; human code review; manual testing; CI/PR review; agent self-report; trace/log review; no consistent method; other.

6. **Which problem has caused the most friction for you?** *(Choose up to two)*  
   Agent spends too much; unclear total cost per issue; wrong task/model choice; repeated retries; output fails tests; hard-to-review changes; lost context after a failure; too much monitoring; can’t tell which agent attempt caused the spend; none so far; other.

7. **How often has an agent task required substantial rework, exceeded your expected cost, or failed its check?** *(Choose one)*  
   Never; once; occasionally; often; almost every time; not sure/not applicable.

8. **What would be the most useful evidence in a tool coordinating coding-agent tasks?** *(Choose up to two)*  
   A task-level cost ceiling; an estimate before launch; visible model/tool activity; a test/verification result; automatic escalation after a failed attempt; a complete attempt ledger; a PR tied back to the task; none of these; other.

9. **If you could change one part of your current workflow, what would you change first?** *(Short answer; optional)*

10. **Would you be open to a short follow-up or a sandbox demo?** *(Choose one)*  
    Yes, I can try a demo; yes, I can talk for 10 minutes; maybe later; no.  
    **Optional contact field shown only for “yes/maybe”:** “How should we contact you?” Use a separate optional field; do not require an email to submit the survey.

### How to use the answers

- Separate answers from people who have used agents recently from general interest. Treat direct examples as stronger evidence than “I might use this.”
- Look for repeated concrete breakdowns: cost attribution, retries, review burden, task choice, or verification. Note counterexamples and users who do not experience the problem.
- Ask 3–5 respondents for a short follow-up if they describe a recent painful incident. Ask what happened, what they did, and what evidence would have helped. Don’t pitch until you understand the incident.
- Share only aggregate, anonymized findings unless a respondent explicitly agrees to be quoted. State the sample size and source; e.g., “4 of 7 respondents who used agents weekly mentioned retry cost,” not “developers agree.”
- Convert one recurring insight into a product decision and post the decision plus reason. If answers don’t support the original premise, say so and adjust.

# Tally architecture graphic — posting and redraw notes

**Files:** `TALLY_ARCHITECTURE_X.svg` (editable vector) and `TALLY_ARCHITECTURE_X.png` (ready to attach).  
**Repository:** inspected public `main` read-only at `a607dc01052ae287fd64ab2a0f1604293005cd4f`, dated 11 October 2026. No repository files were changed.

## How to redraw it

Use a dark 16:9 canvas with pink/violet accents. The top row is the runtime path:

`GitHub issue → Tally control plane → AO worker → repo verifier → GitHub PR`

Inside Tally, show four jobs: **size and route**, **read budget and cap the task**, **run and watch the worker**, **verify and escalate**. Put its local run state and attempt ledger inside the control-plane card.

Under that, use three sponsor cards with distinct colors and arrows to Tally:

- **Entire:** graph/impact signals for task sizing; checkpoints for handoff and recovery.
- **cfo.ai:** read monthly budget, current spend and remaining amount; record spend by run/tier; provide the hackathon business plan for pricing, costs and runway.
- **neatlogs:** capture Tally decisions plus worker model/tool traces; correlate by run/task/attempt; inspect failures. Available pass-rate/cost history can inform tier routing, with local history as fallback.

Finish with a four-step row: **observe → investigate → adjust policy → compare runs**. Label it “human-led today”; the system does not autonomously rewrite its own policy from traces.

## What current `main` actually does

- `engine/real.ts` wires `EntireSizingAdapter`, `EntireCheckpointAdapter`, `EntireCheckpointRecallAdapter`, `CfoaiBudgetAdapter`, `NeatlogsTraceAdapter`, the worker spool/readback, and the GitHub publisher.
- With Entire enabled, graph search/impact supplies sizing signals; checkpoint data can be used for checkpoint recording and escalation context.
- cfo.ai provides the monthly budget/current spend/remaining values and receives spend updates. It is also used for the required business-plan work outside the runtime path.
- Neatlogs records Tally decision/attempt spans and can receive Codex worker spans. `NeatlogsPriceHistory` can aggregate attempt result/cost by task size and tier; `agent/router.ts` consumes history to choose a tier. This is a bounded stats-to-routing path, not general trace interpretation or autonomous policy learning.
- **Caveat before claiming remote history is live:** the current `main` history reader defaults to `limit=100`, while the current Neatlogs Public API docs say trace pages accept at most 50 and use opaque cursors. The adapter catches read errors and falls back to local history. The remote path is optional and should be fixed/verified before describing it as a working feedback loop. See [Neatlogs pagination](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/pagination).

# Tally architecture graphic — posting and redraw notes

**Files:** `TALLY_ARCHITECTURE_X.svg` (editable vector) and `TALLY_ARCHITECTURE_X.png` (ready to attach).  
**Repository:** inspected public `main` read-only at `a607dc01052ae287fd64ab2a0f1604293005cd4f`, dated 11 October 2026. No repository files were changed.

## How to redraw it

Use a dark 16:9 canvas with pink/violet accents. The top row is the runtime path:

`GitHub issue → Tally control plane → AO worker → repo verifier → GitHub PR`

Inside Tally, show four jobs: **size and route**, **read budget and cap the task**, **run and watch the worker**, **verify and escalate**. Put its local run state and attempt ledger inside the control-plane card.

Under that, use three sponsor cards with distinct colors and arrows to Tally:

- **Entire:** graph/impact signals for task sizing; checkpoints for handoff and recovery.
- **cfo.ai:** read monthly budget, current spend and remaining amount; record spend by run/tier; provide the hackathon business plan for pricing, costs and runway.
- **neatlogs:** capture Tally decisions plus worker model/tool traces; correlate by run/task/attempt; inspect failures. Available pass-rate/cost history can inform tier routing, with local history as fallback.

Finish with a four-step row: **observe → investigate → adjust policy → compare runs**. Label it “human-led today”; the system does not autonomously rewrite its own policy from traces.

## What current `main` actually does

- `engine/real.ts` wires `EntireSizingAdapter`, `EntireCheckpointAdapter`, `EntireCheckpointRecallAdapter`, `CfoaiBudgetAdapter`, `NeatlogsTraceAdapter`, the worker spool/readback, and the GitHub publisher.
- With Entire enabled, graph search/impact supplies sizing signals; checkpoint data can be used for checkpoint recording and escalation context.
- cfo.ai provides the monthly budget/current spend/remaining values and receives spend updates. It is also used for the required business-plan work outside the runtime path.
- Neatlogs records Tally decision/attempt spans and can receive Codex worker spans. `NeatlogsPriceHistory` can aggregate attempt result/cost by task size and tier; `agent/router.ts` consumes history to choose a tier. This is a bounded stats-to-routing path, not general trace interpretation or autonomous policy learning.
- **Caveat before claiming remote history is live:** the current `main` history reader defaults to `limit=100`, while the current Neatlogs Public API docs say trace pages accept at most 50 and use opaque cursors. The adapter catches read errors and falls back to local history. The remote path is optional and should be fixed/verified before describing it as a working feedback loop. See [Neatlogs pagination](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/pagination).

Got it—I won’t install it. The npm registry lists **`tally-agents@0.1.0`**, which requires Node 20+ and provides the `tally` command. [npm package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/tally-agents)

```bash
npm install -g tally-agents
tally --help
```

### Try the demo first

Run it in a scratch directory. The demo uses simulated workers and writes its run data there; it doesn’t need GitHub or agent logins.

```bash
mkdir -p ~/tally-smoke
cd ~/tally-smoke
tally demo
```

In another terminal:

```bash
cd ~/tally-smoke
tally dashboard
```

### How a real run works

In your target repo, Tally finds open GitHub issues with the label you configure, estimates task size, selects a model tier, and applies a per-task spending ceiling. It runs the coding agent, checks the configured test command, records the attempt and evidence, then can push a branch and open a PR for review.

For your first real run:

1. Put the `tally` label on just the one issue you want to try, and make sure the repo has a test command that passes.
2. Run `tally init --dry-run` to preview setup. `tally init` asks before applying its proposed repo and runner configuration.
3. Run `tally doctor` to see which prerequisites are ready.
4. Run `tally run --plan` to check the tasks and routing without starting workers or spending.
5. When the plan looks right, run `tally run`. This uses your agent account and may push a branch and open a PR.

The default runner is Agent Orchestrator (AO), which must be installed and running. The alternative is the direct runner, configured with `runner: direct`, which launches Codex or Claude Code itself. Either way, you need GitHub CLI access to the repo and an authenticated coding-agent account. If the RPM you installed is AO, `tally doctor` should tell you whether it’s ready.

### How the integrations fit

- **Entire** can supply repository graph and checkpoint context for sizing and handoffs.
- **Neatlogs** records worker traces and checks whether trace delivery can be read back. The current design uses it for observability and run evidence.
- **cfo.ai** can provide the monthly budget and spend source; `tally login cfoai` connects it.

Each integration is optional and defaults to off in `tally init`. The demo’s `--live` option still uses simulated workers; it only probes read-only integrations.

One small documentation wrinkle: the published package’s README still says it is awaiting publication and has older direct-run proof status. The project’s [current README](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/blob/main/README.md) and [later documentation update](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/commit/74d7231a75a0b607cc6be3fb64fc094175b60221) are newer. | Integration | What it is meant to do | What we proved |

## What Neatlogs is doing

There are two distinct trace paths in Tally:

1. **Tally decision traces.** The code emits events for routing, baseline routing, escalation, and task outcomes. Outcome events include task size, model tier, result, and cost. They use the `tally-cfo-agent` workflow name.
2. **Codex worker traces.** Neatlogs’ Codex hooks can capture the coding session’s model phases, tool calls, and subagent work as a trace tree. Neatlogs documents those hooks as a separate setup that must be trusted in Codex. [Neatlogs Codex Hooks](https://docs.neatlogs.com/integrations/codex)

Tally is **designed to use trace history for later routing**, not just archive it: it looks for measured pass rates and average costs by task size and model tier. With fewer than two usable attempts, it continues using its prior estimate. But the Neatlogs history reader needs a separate service-account read token and project ID; without those, Tally falls back to local `.tally/history.json`.

The service-account token and project ID used for API reads were absent. Neatlogs documents project API keys for ingest and read scopes such as `context:read` and `observability:read` for trace reads. ## Ready for the live runs

I created a **private scratch repo** with six open issues labeled `tally`—two each labeled complex, medium, and menial: [test repo](https://github.com/adot-7/tally-sponsor-e2e-20261011).

I set its run cap to **$5** and pushed that change in commit `bc1fd74`. The no-cost plan schedules all six first attempts for a combined **$4.08** in planned ceilings. It rates both complex and both medium issues as expected, but overestimates both menial issues: #4 is medium and #6 is large. No model workers have run and no model spend has occurred.

### What’s verified so far

- **Neatlogs:** The ingest-key diagnostic sent a trace and verified it was readable back with four spans. That proves the key and backend probe work, but not yet Tally’s decision traces or worker-session hooks.
- **Entire:** The graph plugin is enabled and Tally used graph data when sizing the issues. Its Codex hooks still need trust before we can verify a worker checkpoint.
- **cfo.ai:** Tally’s cached login connected to the MCP server and discovered its tools. I have not read or written any budget tables. The scratch config keeps cfo.ai disabled until the test scenario is ready.
- The scratch app’s baseline had **8 passing tests**.

content.text:
## Issues filed in the main Tally repo

All are open:

- [#120 Neatlogs history pagination](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/issues/120) — requests 100 traces, but the API allows at most 50; the failed read silently falls back to local history.
- [#121 Use configured history in `tally run --plan`](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/issues/121) — planning currently starts with empty in-memory history, so it can disagree with a real run.
- [#122 Preflight models for the active worker account](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/issues/122) — a configured model was rejected before the worker started, while doctor reported ready.
- [#123 Fix cfo.ai onboarding table creation](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/issues/123) — onboarding’s table-create request failed against the live MCP schema; runtime accounting worked after the tables were created manually.
- [#124 Clarify Entire checkpoint sync versus web visibility](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/issues/124) — local capture and GitHub checkpoint refs currently look like they imply Entire Web visibility, but that is a separate setup step.

I left the sizing observation out of the issue list for now: two menial tasks were oversized, which is worth investigating, but two examples are thin evidence of a systematic sizing bug. None of the six final runs escalated, so there’s no escalation failure to report.

## Entire: what’s online now

The checkpoints are **not only local**. The test repo’s `entire status` showed checkpoints syncing to `origin`, and `git ls-remote origin 'refs/entire/checkpoints/*'` returned all six checkpoint refs on the private GitHub repo. That is why `entire checkpoint explain <id>` works locally.

They are **not yet in your Entire Web repository list**. I checked the account logged in as `github:adot-7`: it lists an unrelated `test-repo`, but `entire repo view /gh/adot-7/tally-sponsor-e2e-20261011` found no matching repository, and `entire repo mirror list --available --owner adot-7` returned no GitHub candidates.

To connect it:

1. Install/authorize the [Entire GitHub App](https://entire.io/blog/an-entirely-new-git-hosting-network) for the private test repo. The repo owner or an organization admin needs to grant access.
2. Recheck with `entire repo mirror list --available --owner adot-7`. The test repo should appear once access is granted.
3. Run `entire repo mirror add` and select the repo and region.
4. Verify with `entire repo view /gh/adot-7/tally-sponsor-e2e-20261011 --json`, then find the sessions in Entire Web.

After the repo is visible there, you can share **individual sessions** by setting the selected sessions to Public and copying their links; Entire documents public sharing for sessions from private repos. Review the session contents before sharing, since a session includes agent context. [Entire’s session-sharing guide](https://entire.io/blog/entire-dispatch-0x000d) describes this flow.

The relevant Tally code also reflects the distinction: [Entire onboarding](/home/adot/projects/agentProjects/neatlogs-hack/neatlogs-hack/onboarding/entire.ts) configures local capture and hooks, while [the publisher](/home/adot/projects/agentProjects/neatlogs-hack/neatlogs-hack/adapters/publisher.ts) pushes checkpoint refs to Git remotes. It does not connect a GitHub repo to Entire Web.

## cfo.ai and Neatlogs

**cfo.ai:** The dedicated `Tally E2E` scenario is in the **Included Whippet** workspace. The budget was $5; verified spend was **$1.07277288**, leaving **$3.92722712**. The dedicated [budget ledger](https://app.cfo.ai/s/REDACTED) and [spend detail table](https://app.cfo.ai/s/REDACTED) are there.

Onboarding **does try** to discover or create the two tables, then verify the budget read. That create step failed in this E2E, which is why #123 is filed; runtime reads and writes worked after manual table creation. To show cfo.ai to a sponsor, share the **Tally page** and choose the `Tally E2E` scenario in the Share panel. cfo.ai’s external page links are read-only, can be password-protected, and do not require recipients to sign in. Tables and scenarios themselves are not separately shareable. [cfo.ai sharing instructions](https://docs.cfo.ai/dashboards/share-pages-and-scenarios)

**Neatlogs:** The six worker traces were ultimately read back with spans. Some needed `tally traces drain` and a retry. So trace capture/readback worked; the Neatlogs-backed routing history did **not** reliably work because of the page-size bug. Neatlogs’ current docs specify trace pages of 1–50 with cursor pagination, which is the basis for #120. [Neatlogs pagination docs](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/pagination)

Onboarding does support a Neatlogs ingest key, optional read token/project selection, and worker-hook installation. The ingest key and service-account read token serve different purposes; keep the read token out of messages and demo screenshots. For sponsor viewing, the simplest proof is to open the project and screen-share the traces. Neatlogs’ documented guest links are for evaluation review, rather than general trace browsing. [Neatlogs credential scopes](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/authentication) · [Guest-link endpoints](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/endpoints/guest-links)

The full run-by-run evidence, including all six PRs, costs, trace IDs, and checkpoint IDs, is in the [E2E status report](/tmp/tally-sponsor-e2e-evidence/STATUS.md).

It caps trace pages at Neatlogs’ documented limit of 50, follows opaque cursors for up to 10 pages, and keeps the local fallback while recording remote history failures or empty matches in the run’s Neatlogs status. ([Neatlogs pagination docs](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/pagination))

**Validation:** 670 tests passed, typecheck and build passed, and a read-only live check fetched seven pages using `limit=50` and followed six cursors.

The original checkout’s pre-existing `package-lock.json` edit is untouched. One test environment note: the installed Node 20.20.2 produced an engine warning because Vitest requests Node 22.12 or newer; the tests still passed.

content.text:
Now Neatlogs has two roles in Tally: it shows what happened during a run, and it can supply past results to help choose a model tier for future tasks.

1. **During a real run, Tally sends traces** for routing decisions and escalations. After an attempt, it also sends a structured history record with the task size, tier, result, and cost. Worker traces are drained and checked separately. These let you inspect the run and its decisions in Neatlogs.

2. **On later runs, Tally can read those history records back.** It groups them by task size and tier, then calculates attempt count, pass rate, and average cost. The router uses enough history to estimate whether starting on a cheaper tier is likely to cost less than going straight to the strongest tier. It requires at least two observations by default; with less data, it uses the configured prior instead. The route trace records the decision and its reason.

The history adapter also saves each outcome locally, so Tally can fall back to `.tally/history.json` if Neatlogs has no matching records or the remote read fails. The merged pagination fix lets it read beyond the first 50 traces, and the other merged fix makes `tally run --plan` use the same configured history source as a run. The plan output reports whether its history came from remote Neatlogs, the local fallback, or nowhere.

The important distinction: **Tally uses specific structured attempt records for routing; it doesn’t interpret arbitrary worker-trace contents to decide what model to use.** For this to work remotely, `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` enables trace sending, while `NEATLOGS_TOKEN` and `NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID` enable history reads. A successful Neatlogs integration status and a `remote Neatlogs` plan history source are useful evidence to show in a demo.

content.text:
Yes—Tally **does use Neatlogs trace data to inform routing**. My last paragraph was meant to distinguish *which* traces it uses, but I made that distinction sound like it wasn’t using them.

Tally records structured attempt traces: task size, tier, pass/fail result, and cost. Future routing groups those records by size and tier. Once a group has at least two observations by default, Tally can use its pass rate and the strongest tier’s observed average cost to estimate whether trying a cheaper tier first makes sense. With thinner history, it falls back to configured priors. It doesn’t analyze every detail of the worker’s session trace, and more data gives it better estimates to work with—it doesn’t guarantee every run makes routing more accurate.

**Next issue: #122.** I opened [PR #129](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/pull/129). Since Codex’s model catalog can be bundled rather than an account-access check, Tally now labels configured model access **unverified** in `tally doctor`. If a harness rejects a model, Tally preserves the error and reports the tier, model, and a fix rather than retrying the same model. ([OpenAI docs](https://developers.openai.com/siwc/token-sharing-open-source/codex-app-server); [Claude Code CLI reference](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/cli-usage).) The no-spend limitation is an inference from those documented CLI capabilities.

The full suite passed: **697 tests**, typecheck, and build. GitHub’s release check passed; the PR is open and mergeable. I kept the work in an isolated worktree.

Your X draft has a strong story. I’d make two claims more precise: say the checkpoints preserve *session context* rather than promising the complete context, and describe Neatlogs as using structured attempt history rather than every trace. Also, if you created the cfo.ai tables manually, say Tally connected to and used them.

### Suggested thread

**1/** Update #2 on Tally: our CFO for AI spend.

We pointed Tally at a demo repo with six issues. @EntireHQ’s repo graph helped estimate task scope, and Tally routed each task across low-cost, mid-tier, and top-tier models.

**2/** The bit I love about Entire: checkpoints link commits back to the agent session context behind them. A PR shows the code; a checkpoint helps recover how the change came about. That context is easy to lose when an agent session ends.

**3/** We connected Tally to a dedicated @arithecfo scenario and verified its budget and spend tables. Tally reads the budget and writes tracked spend there. The Ari-in-Slack angle is compelling too: ask about spend and model scenarios without digging through logs.

**4/** @neatlogs traces feed a routing feedback loop. Tally records attempt outcomes and cost, then can use that history to inform future model choices when there are enough observations for a task-size/tier pair. With thin history, it falls back to its priors. We’re excited to test how those estimates improve as evidence builds.

**5/** What should we focus on in the demo: budget caps and escalation, Entire checkpoints, cfo.ai spend tracking, or trace-informed routing?

## Onboarding audit

I tested current `main` in a disposable repo. Init detected `npm test`, let me select direct Codex, leave all sponsor integrations off, set a $5 budget, and review the proposed config before applying it. The generated setup passed all 8 tests. Doctor reported GitHub and Codex connected, integrations off, and model access unverified.

The no-account demo also ran from an empty directory: seven simulated tasks, nine attempts, six passes and one scripted failure. It did not launch a coding agent.

## Improvements to prioritize

1. **Fix AO readiness detection.** On this machine, `ao status` says the daemon is stopped, but pre-init `tally doctor` reports it as connected. Init defaults to AO when the CLI is installed; accepting that default then fails with “AO project API could not be reached.” Choosing direct works. Doctor should check daemon health, and init should make the runner choice reflect that health.

2. **Explain empty plans.** The six demo issues are all linked to open PRs, so Tally correctly excludes them. But `tally run --plan --budget 1` prints only the budget, with no indication that it found zero runnable issues. Show the task count and why issues were excluded.

3. **Make pre-init doctor distinguish optional products.** Before setup, missing AO or sponsor credentials shouldn’t look like blockers when the user can choose direct mode and leave integrations off. After direct setup, the doctor output was clear.

4. **Keep the npm artifact aligned with `main`.** After the package update, smoke-test the published install, and make sure the Getting Started guide is reachable from the packaged README.

content.text:
## Result

PR [#132](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/pull/132) is merged. I tested the merged `main` commit (`4d42683`) from a clean worktree:

- `npm ci`, typecheck, and build passed.
- The test suite passed: **61 files, 724 tests**.
- A fresh local repository completed both interactive and dry-run onboarding. With AO stopped, Tally selected the direct runner, detected the repo’s setup and test commands, and completed initialization. `doctor` then reported GitHub and Codex ready; optional integrations remained off.
- An empty backlog produced a clear “no tasks found” message.

I did not run an issue through to a model-generated change or PR, or write to sponsor services, so this verifies onboarding and readiness—not a full task execution.

## Reproduced first-run failure

The **currently published npm package is still `tally-agents@0.1.0`** and does not include the merged fix. In a clean repo, that installed version fails `tally init --dry-run` when AO is stopped, with: `AO project API could not be reached; start AO and retry.` The merged source handles that same state successfully.

So the remaining first-run problem is a **stale npm release**, rather than a failure in merged `main`. The next step is to publish the merged code under a new package version. Until then, the current `release` branch can be installed with:

```sh
npm install -g 'github:Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack#release'
```

I haven’t filed another issue or published anything. A useful tracking issue, if you want one, would be **“Publish merged first-run onboarding fix to npm.”**

## Repo state and separate follow-up

The current checkout is still on `codex/first-user-integrations` at `ee513f5`; `origin/main` is at `4d42683`. Its only working-tree change is the existing `package-lock.json` modification, which I left untouched. I used temporary repositories under `/tmp` for the onboarding checks.

Separately, `npm audit --omit=dev` reported **14 production dependency advisories** (10 moderate, 4 high). The reported OpenTelemetry and protobuf issues need reachability review before treating them as Tally vulnerabilities: [OpenTelemetry advisory](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-js/security/advisories/GHSA-8988-4f7v-96qf), [protobufjs advisory](https://github.com/protobufjs/protobuf.js/security/advisories/GHSA-66ff-xgx4-vchm). I did not change dependencies; npm’s suggested forced fix would downgrade Neatlogs across a breaking version change.

I want you to do the full complete check in all scenarios and get back to me. just like we did previously for the 6 complex issues we created. this time, we can have lesser number of issues if you want or like issues which cover all three types and also one scenario where it fails on first attempt. and I want you to ensure all sponsor integrations are on and work perfectly. ignore the stale npm release, use the latest, we can update the npm afterwards. no changes to this repo obv.

I’ll run this in an isolated test repo using the latest GitHub release branch, leaving the Tally checkout untouched. I’ll verify setup, each integration, three task sizes, and a deliberate first-attempt failure, then report the actual logs and any gaps. I’ll keep model spend within the previously approved $5 cap and won’t touch the stale npm package.

content.text:
## What I checked

I inspected `origin/main` at `5b48483`. The isolated `tally-agents@0.1.0` build used for the E2E checks is commit `65a760`, whose build message points to that same main commit. I ran the isolated build’s `tally doctor` in the test repo; it reported Entire CLI, Graph, repository capture, and checkpoint recall connected; Neatlogs and cfo.ai connected; and configured model access **unverified**.

No repo files were changed. The existing `package-lock.json` modification is still present.

## 1. Entire verification and the first-failure check

Tally’s Entire verifier runs the configured test command twice: once on the base repo to record a baseline, then on the worker checkout to check for regressions. The baseline command’s exit code is ignored unless Entire itself is unavailable; the candidate result determines pass or fail. That behavior is consistent with Entire Graph’s regression-oriented, adjudicated verification model. See [Tally’s verifier](</tmp/tally-main-5b484-20261012/adapters/verifier.ts:124>) and the [Entire Graph verify reference](https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/blob/main/docs/commands.md).

In the one-shot failure scenario, the test marker was consumed during the **baseline** call. The candidate verification then passed, so the retry/escalation path never received a failed candidate result. This run therefore **does not show that Tally’s retry logic is broken**. In current main, a candidate result of `failed` reaches the escalation decision; a result of `error` does not. See [`engine/real.ts`](</tmp/tally-main-5b484-20261012/engine/real.ts:1177>).

The gap is that Tally does not make the baseline and candidate outcomes clear enough in the saved run. The live scenario was easy to misread as “first attempt failed and Tally didn’t retry.” A controlled test should explicitly make the baseline pass, the candidate fail, and the next candidate pass.

## 2. Neatlogs worker traces

The missing trace was already present in the earlier sponsor E2E. For example, [run `153606Z`](</tmp/tally-sponsor-e2e-20261011/.tally/runs/run-20261011-153606Z/run.json>) recorded “No queued worker trace found.” In the newer run, [ `202804Z`](</tmp/tally-onboarding-e2e-20261012/.tally/runs/run-20261011-202804Z/run.json>) recorded **three retained batches** because another drain held the shared lock; its ledger has a decision `traceId` but `workerTraceId: null`. Other runs did verify worker traces, so this is intermittent rather than a total setup failure.

The current spool code waits up to five seconds for the shared lock and retains batches when delivery cannot be confirmed. The reader retries, but converts non-success HTTP responses to `null` and catches network/auth/processing errors without preserving their cause. That leaves us unable to distinguish missing hooks, a service-token problem, delayed ingestion, another exporter draining the spool, or a trace-correlation miss. See [`neatlogs-worker-spool.ts`](</tmp/tally-main-5b484-20261012/adapters/neatlogs-worker-spool.ts:118>) and [`neatlogs-worker-traces.ts`](</tmp/tally-main-5b484-20261012/adapters/neatlogs-worker-traces.ts:48>).

This was happening before the Entire GitHub App installation. We do not have a fresh Tally worker run after that installation, so current `tally doctor` proves the Neatlogs key is set, but does not prove worker-hook delivery. Neatlogs’ Codex setup also requires the hooks to be loaded and trusted; the read API uses `context:read` and `observability:read` scopes ([Codex hook setup](https://docs.neatlogs.com/integrations/codex), [API scopes](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/authentication)).

The earlier page-size concern does not explain these failures: Neatlogs caps trace-list pages at 50, and Tally requests 50 and follows the cursor. There is a five-page scan bound, which could matter at high trace volume, but it does not match the recorded lock-contention symptom ([pagination docs](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference/pagination)).

## Entire mirroring and Trails

After you installed the Entire GitHub App, the current onboarding E2E repo showed `ready` in Entire, and `entire checkpoint search src/cart.js` returned prior sessions and commits. The older sponsor E2E repo still does not show as onboarded; Entire lists it as **available** to mirror with admin access. The result is repo-specific.

Tally’s Entire onboarding checks login, Graph, and repository capture; it does not create a cloud mirror. Hosted checkpoint recall requires repository access in Entire, while local Graph sizing and capture are separate. The current main `tally doctor` now reports hosted checkpoint recall separately, and it passed for the new E2E repo. See [Tally’s onboarding](</tmp/tally-main-5b484-20261012/onboarding/entire.ts:54>) and [current setup docs](</tmp/tally-main-5b484-20261012/docs/GETTING_STARTED.md:145>). Existing [issue #124](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/issues/124) already tracks the mirror/visibility explanation; update that issue with the new repo-specific evidence rather than opening a duplicate.

Tally has no Entire Trails integration. `entire trail list` returned an empty list for the test repo, and Tally’s code has no Trail creation or linking calls. The CLI environment had no `ENTIRE_PROJECT_TRAILS=1`; current upstream CLI docs put project Trails behind that exact opt-in ([project Trails docs](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/main/docs/architecture/project-trails-cli.md)). I can confirm there are no repo Trails and Tally does not use the feature; I cannot infer an account-level web setting from the CLI.

## Model-account restrictions

The doctor result is deliberately honest: Codex login does not prove access to each selected model, and Tally does not send a potentially billable preflight request. When the worker explicitly reports that a configured model is unavailable, current main turns that into a tier-specific configuration error and tells the user to update `tally.yaml`; it does not silently choose another model. That `error` also skips the normal escalation path. See [`model-access.ts`](</tmp/tally-main-5b484-20261012/engine/model-access.ts:26>) and the [doctor check](</tmp/tally-main-5b484-20261012/engine/doctor.ts:162>).

Tally can handle a model-specific restriction more smoothly with an **explicit opt-in fallback policy**. It should only fall back on a clear model-access rejection, record the requested and actual model, and keep the configured budget and attempt limits. An account-wide quota or usage restriction may affect every model on that account, so changing models would not necessarily help.

## Suggested issues

These are drafts; I did not create them.

### 1. Expose Entire baseline and candidate verification outcomes

**Context:** `EntireGraphVerifier` runs the configured test once on the base repository with `--record-baseline`, then on the worker checkout with `--pre-edit-baseline`. In the first-failure E2E, the one-shot failure marker was consumed by the baseline call; the candidate passed, so no retry/escalation was exercised.

**Acceptance criteria:**

- Record baseline and candidate outcomes separately, including exit status and phase.
- Keep regression-delta behavior, while making a failing baseline visible in run output.
- Add a deterministic test where baseline passes, candidate fails, and a subsequent candidate passes; assert that the normal escalation path runs and the ledger explains why.

This should be framed as a phase-visibility and test-coverage issue, not as a confirmed retry-engine defect.

### 2. Make Neatlogs worker-trace delivery diagnosable and recoverable

**Context:** One earlier run had no queued worker trace; a later run retained three batches after lock contention. Other runs verified traces. The reader suppresses HTTP and network errors, so the saved result cannot identify why readback failed.

**Acceptance criteria:**

- Preserve safe, structured statuses for spool selection, lock wait, export result, and readback.
- Distinguish auth/permission errors, throttling, timeouts, delayed ingestion, correlation misses, and another drain consuming the queue.
- Keep batches queued until confirmed delivered; make recovery report what remains and support bounded retry.
- Cover lock contention, delayed readback, external drain, and failed API responses.
- Keep trace pagination within Neatlogs’ documented 50-item maximum and use cursors.

### 3. Add opt-in fallback for models unavailable to the active account

**Context:** Model access remains unverified until a real attempt. A model-specific rejection currently ends the attempt with a configuration error, without using another configured tier.

**Acceptance criteria:**

- Default to today’s fail-fast behavior.
- Add a user-configured fallback policy for explicit model-unavailable/access-denied errors only.
- Do not fallback on general auth failure, account-wide quota limits, rate limits, or network errors.
- Preserve the requested model, fallback model, reason, cost, and budget accounting in the run evidence.

Current integrations are already opt-in during `tally init`; Neatlogs hooks/read access and Entire capture steps have additional consent. Keep cloud mirroring and any future Trails support explicit too. Existing [issue #88](https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/issues/88) remains the broad first-user-flow tracker; the three drafts above are narrower implementation follow-ups.

I’ll implement the three follow-ups from the analysis: make Entire’s baseline/candidate checks visible, make Neatlogs delivery failures actionable and recoverable, and add a budget-safe opt-in for model-access fallback. I’ll work from a fresh `main` worktree, keep the existing checkout’s `package-lock.json` untouched, run focused tests, then raise the resulting change for review.
